blocks.label: Overview
blocks.text: Learn how to safely update an order API, from deciding the scope of a release to recovery after a failure.

blocks.label: Objective
blocks.text: Choose a deployment method that limits the impact of changes and determine how to recover the application and data when an abnormal event occurs.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Compare the impact on users with the required infrastructure and choose an update method.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Measure the impact on users and decide whether to continue or stop the release.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Compare the time required for recovery with data compatibility and explain the procedure to follow.

blocks.label: Learning objective
blocks.text: You can plan application rollback and database recovery separately.

blocks.label: Choose the deployment scope and switching method
blocks.text: A rolling update is a method of sequentially replacing running tasks with new tasks while keeping the service running. Because old and new tasks run at the same time during the switch, both versions must be able to handle the same APIs and data.

blocks.label: Choose the deployment scope and switching method
blocks.text: With blue/green deployment, you prepare a new environment while keeping the current environment in place, then switch traffic after validation. With a canary deployment, you first send some requests to the updated version and decide whether to switch the remaining traffic based on the results.

blocks.label: Choose the deployment scope and switching method
blocks.text: When choosing, check the capacity that can be secured temporarily, the scope of users affected first, and how quickly you can roll back when something goes wrong. Even if you prepare two environments, the compatibility of data written to the shared database must be considered separately.

steps.label: Choose the deployment scope and switching method

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: The operations team for the order API is releasing a new discount feature. They want to verify it first with only 5% of production requests and reduce the deployment scope if an anomaly occurs.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Verify that the old and new execution environments can handle the same order data.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Send 5% of requests to the updated version and process the rest in the current environment.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Switch the remaining traffic to the updated version only if the predefined observation period has passed and the criteria are met.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can limit the impact if an anomaly occurs while checking the updated version with actual order processing.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: Choosing blue/green lets you roll back safely without checking the data handled by the application.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Even if you can switch back to the original environment, recovery is not possible if the previous version cannot read data written by the updated version. Verify the compatibility of shared data before switching.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Distinguish between replacing tasks and switching the destination for user traffic.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Verify whether the old and new applications running simultaneously can handle the same data.

sources.label: Amazon ECS deployment controllers and strategies

blocks.label: Decide when to expand the release scope and when to abort
blocks.text: Before starting the canary, decide on the observation period, the required data, and the thresholds that will stop the release. For an order API, also check the proportion of orders completed in addition to response time and the HTTP error rate.

blocks.label: Decide when to expand the release scope and when to abort
blocks.text: Overall averages alone can cause you to miss anomalies in the updated version. Separate the metrics for the updated and previous versions and compare them for the same operation. For example, you can use response time at the 95th percentile to capture slow responses.

blocks.label: Decide when to expand the release scope and when to abort
blocks.text: When an abort condition is met, do not proceed to the next stage; the responsible team stops or rolls back the deployment. If the required metrics cannot be collected, do not expand the release scope until the situation can be assessed. In CodeDeploy, configured CloudWatch alarms can be used to decide whether to stop a deployment.

steps.label: Decide when to expand the release scope and when to abort

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: After setting requests to the updated version to 5%, the updated version's order completion rate fell below the predetermined lower limit.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Do not increase the proportion of traffic sent to the updated version, and stop the deployment.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Check the order completion rate, error rate, and response time separately for the updated and previous versions.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: After confirming that the previous version can handle the shared data, return the traffic according to the procedure.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can stop the anomaly before it spreads to all users and record the scope of the impact and the recovery decision.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: If the updated monitoring metrics cannot be retrieved, you can conclude that no abnormality has occurred.

blocks.label: Determine whether no processing has occurred or whether monitoring aggregation has stopped. Do not send new traffic until you can verify the necessary metrics.
blocks.text: Correction

blocks.label: Key points
blocks.text: Decide on the monitoring items, observation period, and stopping conditions before the release.

blocks.label: Key points
blocks.text: Do not rely on overall averages; review the updated and previous versions separately, and distinguish application results from business results.

sources.label: Configuring alarms and rollbacks for AWS CodeDeploy

blocks.label: Choose between rolling back to the previous version and applying a fix
blocks.text: A rollback is the method of returning to the same configuration as the application had before the incident. It is used when the previous version is available and can handle the current data and dependent services. A CodeDeploy rollback redeploys a revision that was deployed previously.

blocks.label: Choose between rolling back to the previous version and applying a fix
blocks.text: If the previous version cannot handle the new data format, another option is to release a fixed version that can read the current data. Decide by comparing the impact of the incident, the scope that can be rolled back, and the time to recovery, including validation.

blocks.label: Choose between rolling back to the previous version and applying a fix
blocks.text: In either case, verify that processing has recovered after the switch. Check not only response times, but also order creation and retrieval, and whether there are duplicate or unprocessed orders.

steps.label: Choose between rolling back to the previous version and applying a fix

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: After releasing an updated version of the order API, an error was found in the price calculation. The updated version stores order data in the same format as the previous version.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Stop expanding the release and confirm that the previous version can use the current configuration and data.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Return traffic to the version that was running before the incident.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Perform order creation and queries, and also check the orders saved during the incident and those requiring reprocessing.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can confirm that the order operations have recovered, not merely that the application has been restored.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: Redeploying the previous version also restores the data written during the incident.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Redeploying the application restores the runtime configuration. Changes to data and operations involving external systems must be investigated separately and recovered as needed.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Before applying the previous version, check compatibility with the data and dependent systems.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: After reverting the route, verify that the actual business operations have recovered.

blocks.label: Make the data structure usable by both the old and new applications
blocks.text: If you rename database columns and switch applications at the same time, the previous version may be unable to read the old columns during the migration. Add the new columns first and create a state in which both the old and new applications can operate during the switch.

blocks.label: Make the data structure usable by both the old and new applications
blocks.text: Move the required data and confirm that the updated version can process it in the new format without problems. Remove the old columns and processing only after there is no longer a possibility of returning to the previous version. If a procedure for restoring the data is needed, decide in advance where to restore it and how to apply the data.

blocks.label: Make the data structure usable by both the old and new applications
blocks.text: When restoring from a backup, simply switching to the restoration target may cause orders placed after the backup was taken to be lost. Validate the restoration procedure and decide how to handle order differences, which data is correct, and when to resume writes.

steps.label: Make the data structure usable by both the old and new applications

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: The order API team is changing the column that stores the delivery address. For a period of time, the old and new applications will use the same database.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Keep the old column and add the new column.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Read and write values with the migrating application, and confirm that it can handle orders in both the old and new formats.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Test the recovery procedure, then stop the previous version before deleting the old column.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: Even if it becomes necessary to use the previous version during the switchover, you can keep the order data usable.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: Publishing the previous version also reverts the database column names and formats to those of the previous version.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: The application and database are changed separately. While the previous version may still be used, ensure data-structure compatibility and prepare restoration as an independent procedure.

blocks.label: Takeaway
blocks.text: Add or migrate first, then remove the old structure after the previous version is no longer needed.

blocks.label: Takeaway
blocks.text: Also validate procedures that handle writes made after the backup.
